case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal court sitting in diversity must enforce Delaware’s medical-malpractice affidavit-of-merit (AOM) requirement (as a prerequisite to maintaining a claim) or instead treat it as displaced by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure under Hanna/Erie.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Delaware medical-malpractice Affidavit-of-Merit (AOM) statute (a state-law requirement that plaintiffs support a malpractice complaint with an expert affidavit/certification early in the case), evaluated through the Erie doctrine and the Rules Enabling Act in relation to Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 3, 8, 9, 11, 12, and 41.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Berk argues Delaware’s AOM requirement cannot be enforced in federal court because it conflicts with, or is foreclosed by, the Federal Rules’ integrated scheme for commencing actions and testing pleading sufficiency—principally Rules 8 and 9 (and also Rule 3 for commencement). In his view, the AOM is effectively an extra, state-imposed evidentiary precondition that raises the federal pleading threshold beyond what the Rules require, functioning like a heightened pleading/proof requirement. Because the Federal Rules occupy the field of what must be filed to begin a civil action and what is required to state a claim, Berk contends the Federal Rules control and Delaware’s AOM must give way; he also resists characterizing the AOM as merely a ‘substantive’ condition under Erie.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Choy/Beebe and supporting amici argue there is no direct collision with any Federal Rule because an AOM is not a ‘pleading’ under Rule 8, and the Delaware requirement operates as a substantive screening/merits-related prerequisite to pursuing professional-negligence claims rather than as a federal pleading rule. Even if analyzed under Erie, they contend the AOM must apply in diversity to avoid forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws, because ignoring it in federal court would create a materially easier path for plaintiffs than Delaware provides in its own courts. They also argue Petitioner’s approach improperly treats any potential overlap as preemption and would require revisiting settled Hanna-line cases; respondents emphasize the Court’s precedents allowing state provisions to operate alongside the Federal Rules where both can be sensibly applied (including applying Federal Rules in a way that preserves substantive state policy where possible).
key_precedents: Shady Grove Orthopedic Associates, P.A. v. Allstate Insurance Co.
Gasperini v. Center for Humanities, Inc.
Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp.
Semtek International Inc. v. Lockheed Martin Corp.

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point—that Rules 3 and 8 comprehensively regulate commencement and pleading and therefore displace any added state “certificate” requirement—still reads those Rules at too high a level of generality and would turn ordinary federal pleading provisions into broad preemptive commands. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, none of Rules 3, 8, 9, 11, 12, or 41 is “sufficiently broad to control the issue” Delaware addresses—whether a plaintiff may maintain a Delaware med-mal claim absent early expert attestation—so we can follow Gasperini/Semtek’s reconciliation approach rather than declare a Hanna/Shady Grove collision. Justice Gorsuch’s Rules Enabling Act concern reinforces the institutional hazard: construing the Rules to nullify the AOM would effectively enlarge the substantive availability of the state-created claim in federal court, which we should avoid absent an on-point federal command. A narrow holding applying Delaware’s AOM as a state condition on suit in diversity best serves Erie’s twin aims and preserves the legitimacy of the Federal Rules by not overextending them.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Rules 3 and 8 (and perhaps 12) comprehensively specify what must be filed to commence and test a civil action, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement “adds” an impermissible federal pleading prerequisite. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, that frames the Federal Rules at too high a level of generality: their text governs federal pleadings and timing, not whether Delaware has defined the very availability of its own malpractice cause of action to include an early expert attestation. Justice Gorsuch’s Rules Enabling Act concern is decisive under a textualist approach—reading Rules 3 or 8 to nullify the AOM would effectively enlarge the substantive entitlement to sue on a Delaware-created claim in federal court, which the Act forbids absent a clear textual command. Semtek and Gasperini, which several colleagues invoked, reinforce construing the Rules narrowly to avoid displacing substantive state policy where no Rule squarely answers the same question, so I continue to see no “direct collision” under Hanna/Shady Grove.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Rules 3 and 8 are “sufficiently broad” to govern commencement and pleading, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit (AOM) necessarily collides under Hanna/Shady Grove; but that argument depends on reading the Federal Rules at an impermissibly high level of generality. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, the Rules specify what a federal complaint must contain and when an action is commenced for federal purposes; they do not purport to negate state-law conditions that define the availability of a state-created medical-malpractice claim, so there is no unavoidable direct collision. Justice Gorsuch’s Rules Enabling Act concern further reinforces my view: construing the Rules to displace the AOM would effectively enlarge the plaintiff’s substantive entitlement to pursue a Delaware claim in federal court, which we should avoid where the federal text does not clearly compel that result. Under Erie’s twin aims, exempting diversity plaintiffs from the AOM would predictably invite forum shopping and inequitable administration, so the AOM should apply alongside the Federal Rules.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Rules 3 and 8 set the full federal baseline for commencing an action and stating a claim, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement must "collide" and fall under Hanna/Shady Grove. But I agree with Justice Kagan (and Justice Barrett) that this frames the Federal Rules at too high a level of generality: they regulate what a federal complaint must contain and when the federal clock starts, not whether Delaware has substantively conditioned the continued maintenance of its med-mal cause of action on early expert support. Justice Gorsuch’s Rules Enabling Act concern strengthens my view that reading Rules 3/8 to displace the AOM would effectively enlarge the state-law entitlement to sue in federal court, something we should avoid where, as Semtek/Gasperini suggest, a reasonable reconciliation exists. Under Erie’s twin aims and my pragmatic focus on real-world consequences, exempting diversity plaintiffs from the AOM would predictably invite forum shopping and distort Delaware’s calibrated screening mechanism in a way that undermines fairness and equal treatment of similarly injured patients across forums.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains that Rules 3 and 8 are “sufficiently broad” to control commencement and pleading, so any state affidavit-of-merit requirement must yield under Hanna/Shady Grove; but that pitches the Federal Rules at too high a level of generality and misidentifies the “issue” the Rules actually answer. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, the Rules specify what a federal complaint must contain and when an action is commenced for federal purposes, while Delaware’s AOM is better understood as a state-law precondition to maintaining a state-created malpractice claim—something the Rules do not purport to eliminate. Justice Gorsuch’s Rules Enabling Act concern matters here: construing Rules 3/8 to displace the AOM would effectively expand the practical availability of Delaware’s claim in federal court, a result we should avoid where the texts can be reconciled. And under Erie’s twin aims, exempting diversity plaintiffs from the AOM would predictably invite forum shopping by making federal court materially easier for the same Delaware claim.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Rules 3, 8, and 12 comprehensively regulate commencement, pleading, and testing sufficiency, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit looks like an extra federal “pleading” hurdle; but that framing reads the Federal Rules at an impermissibly high level of generality and ignores their actual text. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett persuasively note, the Rules specify what a complaint must contain and how motions operate in federal court, not whether Delaware may define the availability of its own malpractice cause of action by requiring an early expert attestation as a condition to maintain the claim. Justice Alito’s Rules Enabling Act concern reinforces the textual analysis: construing the Rules to nullify the AOM would effectively enlarge the plaintiff’s entitlement to pursue a Delaware-created claim in federal court, which the Act forbids and which Shady Grove’s Stevens concurrence cautions against. With no unavoidable “direct collision,” Gasperini/Semtek-style reconciliation and Erie’s twin aims counsel applying the AOM to avoid creating a materially easier federal forum for the same state claim.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Rules 3 and 8 comprehensively govern commencing an action and what must be filed, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit looks like an added pleading prerequisite that should fall under Hanna. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, that frames the Federal Rules at too high a level of generality: the Rules specify what a federal complaint must contain and when an action is commenced for federal purposes, not whether Delaware has conditioned the availability/maintenance of its med-mal cause of action on early expert support. Justice Gorsuch’s Rules Enabling Act concern (echoing Shady Grove’s Stevens concurrence) strengthens the institutionalist, narrower path—reading the Rules to displace the AOM would effectively enlarge the state-created claim in federal court, which we should avoid where reconciliation is plausible under Semtek/Gasperini. Applying the AOM in diversity also better serves Erie’s twin aims by reducing forum shopping and inequitable administration without rewriting any Federal Rule’s text.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains that Rules 3 and 8 (and perhaps 12) are “sufficiently broad” to control what must be filed to commence and maintain a federal civil action, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit necessarily collides. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, that frames the Federal Rules at an impermissibly high level of generality: the Rules specify the contents of pleadings and the timing effects of filing, not whether Delaware has defined its malpractice cause of action to be unavailable absent early expert support. Justice Gorsuch’s Rules Enabling Act point is also decisive for me—construing Rules 3/8 to displace the AOM would risk enlarging the substantive availability of a Delaware claim in federal court, contrary to the Act and consistent with Justice Stevens’s Shady Grove concurrence. With no unavoidable “direct collision,” Gasperini and Semtek counsel a reconciliatory reading that applies the AOM to serve Erie’s twin aims and avoid forum shopping.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Rules 3, 8, and 12 comprehensively regulate commencement, pleading, and dismissal, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement “collides” by forcing dismissal for a missing filing. But, as Justice Kagan and the Chief emphasize, that framing treats the Federal Rules at too high a level of generality: the Rules specify what a federal complaint must contain and how defenses are raised, not whether Delaware may condition the continued maintenance of its malpractice cause of action on early expert support. Justice Gorsuch’s Rules Enabling Act concern further strengthens my view that reading Rules 3/8 to displace the AOM would effectively enlarge the substantive availability of a Delaware claim in federal court, which is precisely what we should avoid where a workable reconciliation exists (consistent with Semtek/Gasperini). Under Erie’s twin aims, exempting diversity plaintiffs from the AOM would predictably create forum-shopping pressure and inequitable administration, so I remain with Respondent.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Hanna and Burlington Northern, the threshold question is whether any Federal Rule is “sufficiently broad” to control the issue and thus create a “direct collision” with Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit prerequisite; Rules 3, 8, 9, 11, 12, and 41 govern commencement, pleading, sanctions, motions, and dismissals, but none purports to answer whether a state may require an early expert certification as a condition of maintaining a medical-malpractice claim. Because the AOM is not itself a “pleading” within Rule 8 and can operate alongside federal pleading and motion practice without rewriting the Rules, this case fits the Court’s line of decisions (including Gasperini and Semtek) counseling reconciliation where possible to respect substantive state policy. Applying Delaware’s AOM in diversity also advances Erie’s aims by avoiding forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws, akin to Woods and Cohen’s recognition that certain state-law litigation prerequisites or conditions on suit apply in federal court when they do not collide with a Federal Rule. A narrow holding enforcing Delaware’s AOM as a substantive precondition to maintaining the claim best preserves precedent and institutional legitimacy without inviting wholesale reconsideration of the Hanna framework.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Nothing in the text of Rules 3, 8, 9, 11, 12, or 41 purports to forbid a State from conditioning the maintenance of a medical-malpractice claim on an early expert certification; those Rules govern federal pleading and motion practice, but they do not answer the same question as Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit prerequisite. Under Hanna and Shady Grove, the Federal Rules displace state law only upon a true “direct collision,” and reading Rules 8 or 3 to preempt any additional state-law prerequisites would stretch their text beyond their ordinary meaning and trench on state authority over substantive tort policy. Applying Delaware’s AOM in diversity also accords with Erie’s twin aims by preventing forum shopping and inequitable administration, consistent with decisions like Woods and Cohen that require federal courts to respect state-created limits on who may maintain certain state-law causes of action. Because the AOM functions as a state-defined condition on the availability of the malpractice cause of action, enforcing it does not abridge any federally conferred procedural entitlement under the Rules Enabling Act.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Delaware’s AOM requirement can operate alongside the Federal Rules because it is not a “pleading” rule within the meaning of Rules 8 or 9, but a state-law condition on maintaining a medical-malpractice claim, and thus there is no “direct collision” under Hanna v. Plumer and Burlington Northern R. Co. v. Woods. Properly read, Rule 3 governs commencement of an action for federal timing purposes, but it does not purport to forbid States from attaching substantive preconditions to particular causes of action; treating Rule 3 or Rule 8 as implicitly preempting such prerequisites would be an unwarranted, atextual expansion of the Rules. Even if one proceeds to Erie’s twin aims, refusing to apply the AOM statute in diversity would invite forum shopping and create inequitable administration by allowing plaintiffs to evade Delaware’s expert-screening requirement simply by choosing federal court. This result also accords with the Rules Enabling Act limitation, reflected in Justice Stevens’s Shady Grove concurrence, because construing the Federal Rules to displace Delaware’s AOM would risk enlarging plaintiffs’ substantive ability to pursue malpractice claims free of the State’s merits-screening condition.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement can operate alongside the Federal Rules because it does not “direct[ly] collid[e]” with Rules 3, 8, or 9: those Rules govern commencement and the content of pleadings, while the AOM is a state-law, merits-screening prerequisite for maintaining a medical-malpractice claim rather than a heightened federal pleading rule. Under Hanna and Burlington Northern’s “scope … sufficiently broad to control the issue” test, the Rules are not so comprehensive here as to leave “no room” for the AOM’s operation, especially where the statute functions like other state conditions on suit that federal courts have applied in diversity. Applying the AOM also advances Erie’s twin aims by preventing forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws—avoiding a regime where plaintiffs could bypass Delaware’s early expert-screening simply by filing in federal court. This approach is consistent with Gasperini and Semtek’s instruction to apply federal procedure in a manner that preserves substantive state policy where feasible, and it avoids converting the Federal Rules into an engine for diluting state protections governing professional-liability claims.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Delaware’s AOM statute can operate alongside the Federal Rules because none of Rules 3, 8, 9, 11, 12, or 41 is “sufficiently broad to cause a direct collision” with a state-law prerequisite requiring an early expert certification in medical-malpractice cases. Under Hanna and Burlington Northern, the Federal Rules govern pleadings and case management in federal court, but they do not purport to eliminate state substantive conditions on maintaining particular state-created claims; as in Cohen and Woods, diversity plaintiffs may be held to state-law preconditions that screen the merits and affect access to the state-law cause of action. And even if the question is framed in Erie terms, declining to apply the AOM would invite forum shopping and produce inequitable administration by making Delaware malpractice suits materially easier in federal court than in Delaware court, contrary to Erie’s core aims and consistent with Gasperini’s instruction to accommodate state substantive policy where workable.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement can operate alongside the Federal Rules because no Federal Rule squarely answers the same question—whether a plaintiff may maintain a state-created medical-malpractice claim without an early expert attestation. Rules 3, 8, and 9 specify how an action is commenced and what a pleading must contain, but they do not confer a right to proceed absent state-law preconditions to suit; treating the AOM as displaced would effectively enlarge the plaintiff’s entitlement to pursue a Delaware malpractice claim in federal court, raising the Rules Enabling Act concern highlighted in Justice Stevens’s controlling concurrence in Shady Grove. Under Erie’s twin aims, refusing to apply the AOM would invite forum shopping and produce inequitable administration by making federal court materially more permissive than Delaware court for the same claim, consistent with cases like Woods and Cohen recognizing the applicability of substantive state conditions on suit in diversity. Where possible we should read the Federal Rules to avoid such displacement of state substantive policy, much as Semtek construed Rule 41 in a manner that preserves state law consequences rather than overriding them.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Hanna and Burlington Northern v. Woods, the threshold question is whether any Federal Rule is “sufficiently broad” to control the issue and thus create a direct collision; Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement can operate alongside Rules 3, 8, 9, 11, and 12 because it does not redefine what a “pleading” must contain under Rule 8, but instead imposes a state-law prerequisite to maintaining a Delaware medical-malpractice claim. Where the Federal Rules can be sensibly applied without displacing a substantial state policy choice, our precedents favor that path (Gasperini; Semtek), especially in diversity where ignoring the AOM would invite forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws (Erie; Woods). Even if there is some overlap, Shady Grove counsels against reading Federal Rules at an artificially high level of generality to nullify state conditions that define the practical availability of a claim, absent a clear, unavoidable conflict. Respecting Delaware’s AOM requirement here is the narrower, more workable approach that preserves both federal procedural uniformity and the State’s substantive screening regime without expanding the Federal Rules beyond their proper procedural domain under the Rules Enabling Act.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Hanna and Burlington Northern, the threshold question is whether any Federal Rule is “sufficiently broad” to control the issue and thus cause a direct collision with Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit prerequisite; Rules 3, 8, 9, 11, 12, and 41 regulate commencement, pleadings, sanctions, and dismissal procedure, but none purports to specify the substantive preconditions Delaware attaches to maintaining a medical-malpractice claim. An AOM is not a “pleading” within Rules 7–9, and reading Rules 8 or 3 to impliedly forbid any state-law merit-screening condition would stretch their text beyond their ordinary meaning and disregard the settled practice, reflected in cases like Gasperini and Cohen, of accommodating substantive state policies alongside the Federal Rules where both can operate. With no direct conflict, Erie’s twin aims counsel applying the Delaware requirement in diversity to prevent forum shopping and inequitable administration, since disregarding the AOM would create a materially easier path in federal court than in Delaware courts. Because the AOM operates as a merits-related gatekeeping condition rather than as an alternative federal pleading standard, it should be enforced absent a valid, on-point Federal Rule that displaces it.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Applying Hanna and Burlington Northern’s “direct collision” test, Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement can operate alongside the Federal Rules because it does not purport to redefine what a “pleading” must contain under Rules 8 and 9 or when an action is “commenced” under Rule 3; it instead functions as a state-law precondition to maintaining a medical-malpractice claim, with dismissal consequences that do not inherently contradict Rules 12 or 41. Under Erie’s forum-shopping and inequitable-administration concerns (Woods; Cohen), ignoring Delaware’s AOM would create a materially easier federal path for med-mal plaintiffs than exists in Delaware courts, undermining equal treatment and the State’s substantive screening policy. Consistent with Gasperini and Semtek, the Federal Rules should be applied in a manner that preserves substantive state policy where feasible rather than treating any overlap as displacement. Because there is no unavoidable conflict with a valid Federal Rule, the state requirement applies in diversity.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a federal court sitting in diversity must enforce Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit (AOM) requirement for medical-negligence claims, or whether the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure displace it under Hanna/Erie because it conflicts with the Rules’ pleading and filing framework.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Delaware’s medical-negligence affidavit-of-merit statute (AOM requirement) as applied in federal diversity litigation, analyzed through the Erie doctrine and the Rules Enabling Act/Hanna framework in relation to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (especially Rules 3, 8, 9, 11, and 12).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Berk argues that Delaware’s AOM regime cannot be enforced in federal court because it conflicts with the Federal Rules’ comprehensive scheme for commencing an action and stating a claim. He contends that Rules 8 and 9 define what is required to plead a claim in federal court and implicitly forbid conditioning suit on submitting extra-pleading evidence (an expert affidavit). He also suggests a conflict with Rule 3’s rule for commencing an action, and argues that Rule 11 already addresses frivolous filings—making a state-law affidavit gatekeeping device incompatible with the federal approach. In his view, once a valid Federal Rule answers the question, Hanna requires applying the Federal Rule, which would mean the AOM requirement is displaced in federal diversity cases.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Choy and Beebe Medical Center argue that Delaware’s AOM requirement is enforceable in federal court because it does not directly collide with any Federal Rule: it is not a pleading rule (so it does not conflict with Rules 8 or 9), and it operates as a substantive state-law precondition/filter for professional-negligence suits that Erie requires federal courts to respect to avoid outcome-determinative forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws. They further contend that accepting petitioner’s theory would require an improper, facial invalidation approach (treating a state statute as displaced if it could conflict in some hypothetical application), contrary to this Court’s post-Hanna precedents. Respondents also emphasize that Delaware’s scheme advances legitimate state policy goals (screening meritless med-mal suits, protecting access to care) without rewriting the Federal Rules.

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains that Rules 8 and 11 comprehensively occupy pleading sufficiency and prefiling inquiry, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit must fall under Hanna/Shady Grove; but that argument still depends on reading the Rules as an exclusivity regime they do not textually claim to be. As Justice Kagan persuasively emphasized, an affidavit is not a “pleading,” and Rules 8/11 regulate what must be in the complaint and what counsel certifies—not whether a State may attach an expert-certification condition to maintaining a state-created med-mal claim. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Cohen and Woods reinforces that we have long applied state-law preconditions on access to suit in diversity absent a true “direct collision,” and a Semtek/Gasperini-style narrowing construction avoids turning the Federal Rules into an on/off switch that would invite forum shopping. I would keep the holding narrow: Delaware’s AOM is a claim-specific substantive precondition enforceable through ordinary federal dismissal practice, without rewriting the Federal Rules.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest contention—that Rules 8 and 11 comprehensively occupy pleading sufficiency and prefiling certification and therefore displace Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit—fails on the Rules’ text: Rule 8 specifies what a "pleading" must contain, and Rule 11 regulates the representations made by signing papers; neither purports to forbid States from attaching an expert-certification condition to a state-created medical-negligence claim. As Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, no Federal Rule is "sufficiently broad" to answer the distinct question Delaware addresses, so there is no Hanna/Shady Grove “direct collision,” and an originalist/textualist reading does not stretch the Rules into an implied exclusivity regime. The Chief Justice’s Semtek point reinforces the proper interpretive move here: construe the Federal Rules narrowly where their text permits so they do not unnecessarily displace substantive state calibrations of liability, and our precedents (including Cohen and Woods) support applying state-law prerequisites in diversity to avoid forum shopping and inequitable administration. I therefore adhere to my vote for respondent.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest contention remains that Rules 8 and 11 form an exclusive federal pleading-and-screening code, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit necessarily “collides” by adding an extra hurdle; but as Justice Kagan persuasively notes, an affidavit is not a “pleading,” and Rule 11 is a sanctions mechanism rather than a guarantee of access to a state-created cause of action without satisfying state conditions. Chief Justice Roberts’s Semtek-style narrowing construction is the right approach: absent a clear textual overlap, we should not read the Federal Rules as an on/off switch that displaces state substantive gatekeeping devices. Justice Thomas’s invocation of Cohen and Woods further supports applying Delaware’s prerequisite in diversity because it functions as a condition on maintaining the claim and ignoring it would invite forum shopping and inequitable administration. Nothing in the colleagues’ discussion identifies a Federal Rule “sufficiently broad” to control the same issue, so my vote stays with respondent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains that Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit functions as an added gateway that can screen out injured patients—often those with fewer resources—despite Rule 8’s notice-pleading regime and Rule 11’s certification framework. But Justice Kagan’s observation that an affidavit is not a “pleading,” combined with Chief Justice Roberts’s Semtek-informed warning against treating the Federal Rules as an on/off switch, persuades me that Rules 3/8/11/12 are not “sufficiently broad” to answer the same question Delaware answers—whether this state-created claim may be maintained absent expert support. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Cohen and Woods strengthens the Erie analysis: we have applied state-law conditions on access to state remedies in diversity when no Federal Rule directly collides, and ignoring Delaware’s screening device would predictably generate forum shopping and unequal treatment of similarly situated Delaware patients. Although I remain troubled by the access-to-justice burdens, my pragmatic approach cuts against creating a federal-court carveout that systematically advantages diversity plaintiffs over in-state plaintiffs under the same substantive tort regime.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Rules 8 and 11 supply a comprehensive federal pleading-and-screening scheme, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit looks like an added front-end hurdle. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, those Rules regulate what a “pleading” must contain and what an attorney certifies by signing papers; they do not purport to answer the distinct question Delaware addresses—whether this state-created med-mal claim may be maintained absent an external expert attestation—so there is no Hanna/Shady Grove “direct collision.” Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Justice Stevens’s Shady Grove concurrence reinforces a narrow, text-grounded collision inquiry that avoids turning the Federal Rules into an implied exclusivity regime displacing state substantive gatekeeping. And Justice Thomas’s invocation of Cohen and Woods matters: those cases confirm we routinely apply state-law suit prerequisites in diversity when no Rule squarely controls, which also better serves Erie’s anti–forum-shopping and equitable-administration aims here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest contention remains that Rules 8 and 11 occupy the field of federal pleading and prefiling certification, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit necessarily conflicts; but that argument still depends on reading those Rules as an exclusivity guarantee they do not textually supply. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, the Federal Rules answer what a pleading must contain and how federal courts police improper filings, while Delaware’s statute answers a different question—whether this state-created claim may be maintained without an expert-supported attestation—so there is no Hanna/Shady Grove “direct collision.” Justice Thomas’s reliance on Cohen and Woods is persuasive in framing this as a state-law precondition materially defining access to the remedy, which Erie’s twin aims counsel us to apply to avoid forum shopping and unequal administration. Nothing in the colleagues’ discussion identifies a Rule “sufficiently broad” to control this issue and leave no room for Delaware’s claim-specific gatekeeping, so I remain with respondent.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Rules 8 and 11 create a comprehensive federal pleading-and-screening regime, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit (AOM) necessarily conflicts under Hanna/Shady Grove. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, the Rules regulate what a complaint must contain and the consequences of signing papers; they do not purport to answer the distinct state-law question whether a particular state-created med-mal claim may be maintained absent an expert-backed attestation, so there is no “direct collision.” Justice Barrett’s Cohen/Woods analogy strengthens my view that this is properly understood as a claim-specific condition on access to the state remedy, and construing the Federal Rules to preempt it would extend Shady Grove beyond Justice Stevens’s limiting approach and invite the forum shopping Erie seeks to prevent. I therefore remain with the respondent and would favor a narrow holding emphasizing the AOM’s non-pleading character and enforceability through ordinary federal dismissal mechanisms.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Petitioner’s best contention remains that Rules 8 and 11 comprehensively occupy the field of initiating and screening federal suits, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit “collides” by adding a further threshold. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the Rules speak to the content of pleadings and the consequences of signing papers; they do not purport to answer the distinct question Delaware addresses—whether this state-created medical-negligence claim may be maintained absent an external expert attestation—so there is no Hanna/Shady Grove direct collision on the Rules’ text. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Justice Stevens’s Shady Grove concurrence reinforces that we should not read the Federal Rules as an on/off switch displacing a state provision tightly bound to the substantive calibration of a remedy absent clear textual overlap. With no genuine collision, Erie’s twin aims and precedents like Cohen and Woods (highlighted by Justice Thomas) support applying the AOM to avoid forum shopping and inequitable administration.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point remains that Rules 8 and 11 set the field for initiating suit and policing weak claims, so Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit (AOM) is an extra federal hurdle; but that framing assumes the Rules are “sufficiently broad” to answer the distinct question Delaware asks—whether this state-created med-mal cause of action may be maintained absent expert support. Justice Kagan’s observation that an affidavit is not a “pleading,” and that Rule 11 is a sanctions regime rather than an exclusivity guarantee, is decisive for me under Hanna/Shady Grove because it eliminates the claimed direct collision. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Cohen and Woods also matters: those cases underscore that certain state-law preconditions operate as substantive limits on the remedy, and ignoring them in diversity predictably invites forum shopping and unequal administration. On pragmatic consequences, exempting diversity plaintiffs from the AOM would create a two-track Delaware med-mal system, undermining procedural fairness for similarly situated patients and providers depending only on forum selection.

John Roberts.reasoning: Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement can be applied in federal diversity actions because it does not “directly collide” with any Federal Rule: Rules 8 and 9 govern what must appear in a pleading, while the AOM operates as a state-law precondition to maintaining a medical-negligence claim and can be enforced through federal mechanisms (e.g., dismissal) without rewriting the Rules. Under Burlington Northern and this Court’s Erie cases, we avoid treating the Federal Rules as an “on/off switch” that displaces state substantive screening regimes absent a clear conflict, an approach reinforced by Semtek’s instruction to construe Federal Rules to preserve substantive state policies where fairly possible. Applying the AOM requirement also advances Erie’s core aims by reducing forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws, consistent with Cohen and Woods, and a narrow holding enforcing the Delaware statute in this context best serves institutional legitimacy and federalism.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under Erie and the Rules Enabling Act, a Federal Rule displaces state law only if it genuinely answers the same question and is valid; Rules 3, 8, 9, 11, and 12 govern how to commence an action and what a federal pleading must contain, but they do not purport to forbid state-law, outside-the-complaint preconditions to pursuing a state-created medical-negligence claim. Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement functions like the state-law bond and other preconditions this Court enforced in diversity in Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. and Woods v. Interstate Realty Co.—it does not add allegations to the complaint but instead conditions continued prosecution of a particular state-law cause of action. Because there is no direct collision with any Federal Rule (cf. Samuel Alito.reasoning: Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement can be applied in diversity because there is no “direct collision” with the Federal Rules: Rules 8 and 9 govern what must be alleged in a pleading, while the AOM is a separate state-law precondition for maintaining a medical-negligence action and does not purport to redefine federal pleading content. Under the Burlington Northern/Woods formulation (reaffirmed in Shady Grove’s conflict analysis), a Federal Rule displaces state law only when it is sufficiently broad to control the issue and leave no room for the state provision; Rules 3 and 11 do not confer a right to proceed without satisfying substantive state screening devices. Enforcing the AOM also avoids the forum-shopping and inequitable administration concerns that Erie and cases like Cohen v. Beneficial and Woods v. Interstate Realty sought to prevent when states condition access to their causes of action. Because the Rules can operate alongside the AOM without rewriting their text, the state requirement should be respected as part of the substantive regime Delaware has attached to med-mal claims.

Under Hanna and Burlington Northern’s “direct collision” inquiry—reaffirmed as “familiar” in Shady Grove—the Federal Rules are not so broad as to leave “no room” for Delaware’s screening mechanism, so Erie’s twin aims (discouraging forum shopping and avoiding inequitable administration of the laws) favor enforcing the AOM in diversity. This is especially so given our precedents treating similar state-law conditions on suit as applicable in federal court to preserve substantive state policy choices about access to particular remedies, see Cohen and Woods.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit statute functions as a state-law precondition to maintaining a medical-negligence action, and none of Rules 3, 8, 9, 11, or 12 is “sufficiently broad” to answer the same question so as to create a “direct collision” leaving “no room” for the state rule. Because applying the AOM requirement in diversity materially affects the availability of a Delaware medical-negligence claim and prevents forum shopping and inequitable administration, Erie supports enforcement absent a true Rules conflict, consistent with Cohen and Woods.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Delaware’s affidavit-of-merit requirement functions as a state-law precondition to maintaining a medical-negligence action, and it does not “direct[ly] collid[e]” with Rules 3, 8, 9, 11, or 12 under Hanna and Burlington Northern because those Rules govern commencing an action and the sufficiency of pleadings, not whether state law conditions the availability of the claim on an expert-supported certification. Procedural fairness and practical consequences also favor enforcement here: exempting federal plaintiffs from the AOM gatekeeping requirement would predictably shift med-mal filings into federal court and create unequal treatment of similarly situated Delaware litigants based solely on forum.
